goal: how to set up bullet points
preamble: A bulleted list looks like a row of dots you could type yourself, but Docs doesn't see dots. It sees a paragraph that has been told it is a list item. Once a line knows that about itself, the bullet, the indent, and the spacing all follow automatically — and every new line you press Enter on inherits the same rule. So you're not decorating text here. You're changing what kind of paragraph it is.
generalization: The toolbar bullet button would have given you one bullet style with no questions asked. Going through Format instead showed you the thing the button was hiding: a list is a paragraph property with options, not a character you insert. That's why the bullet survives when you reorder lines, why pressing Tab nests it, and why deleting the text doesn't leave a stray dot behind.

steps.intent: Bullets aren't something you add to a document — they're a decision about how an existing paragraph behaves. The menu that deals with how text and paragraphs behave, rather than what's in them, is where this starts.
hints: You're not putting anything new on the page. You're changing the nature of a line that's already there — which menu owns that?
The menu bar along the top, between Insert and Tools.

wrongHints.Insert: Insert is for things that weren't in the document before — images, tables, page breaks. A bullet isn't a new object; it's a property of a paragraph you already have.
wrongHints.Tools: Tools holds things that act on the document from outside — spelling, word count, voice typing. Formatting a paragraph is Format's job.

steps.intent: Docs keeps every kind of list under one roof, because bulleted and numbered lists are the same mechanism wearing different clothes. Open the group that names both.
hints: Bullets and numbers are two answers to the same question, so Docs files them together under one entry.
Middle of the Format menu, below the spacing options.

wrongHints.Paragraph styles: That's headings and body text — what a paragraph means in the document's structure. A list is about how the paragraph is laid out, not what rank it holds.
wrongHints.Align & indent: Reasonable guess, since bullets indent. But indenting only moves text sideways; it won't make Docs treat the line as a list item or carry the bullet to the next line.
wrongHints.Line & paragraph spacing: Spacing controls the gaps between lines. It'll change how the list breathes once it exists, but it can't create one.

steps.intent: Now you pick which of the two list types you want. Bullets say the order doesn't matter; numbers say it does. That distinction is the only real difference between these two branches.
hints: Your items have no first, second, third about them — they're just a set. Choose the branch that says so.
The first of the two list types in the submenu that just opened.

wrongHints.Numbered list menu: Numbers imply sequence — steps, rankings, things that must happen in order. If the items could be shuffled without losing meaning, bullets are the honest choice.
wrongHints.List options: That's for adjusting a list you already have — restarting numbering, editing prefixes. There's no list here yet to adjust.

steps.intent: Your turn, with no highlight. What opened is a small grid of bullet shapes — the same mechanism every time, just a different mark. Pick the plain one in the top-left corner: it's the default Docs uses everywhere, which means your list will match anything else in the document.
hints: They all do the identical thing. Choose the one that draws the least attention to itself — the one you've seen in every document you've ever read.
First row, first column of the grid that just appeared.
